questions.topic: Term Frequency and Its Saturation Problem
questions.question: What is raw term frequency?
options: The number of times a given term occurs inside one particular document
The number of documents in the collection that contain the term
The number of distinct terms the document contains after analysis
The number of times a term occurs across the entire collection

questions.topic: Term Frequency and Its Saturation Problem
questions.question: What is the central defect of linear raw term frequency?
options: It assumes the first occurrence carries no evidence until a term repeats
It treats the tenth occurrence as exactly as informative as the very first
It caps each term's contribution once the count passes a fixed ceiling
It discards repeated occurrences and keeps only presence information

questions.question: Using 1 plus natural log tf, what weight does tf equal to 1 receive?

questions.topic: Term Frequency and Its Saturation Problem
questions.question: Why does logarithmic tf reduce keyword-stuffing influence?
options: Each extra occurrence adds less weight than the occurrence before it did
Every occurrence after the first contributes nothing once a log is applied
The transform subtracts the collection mean frequency from every raw count
The weight decreases again once the count rises above the corpus average

questions.topic: Term Frequency and Its Saturation Problem
questions.question: Which tf choice best fits an unordered tag field where repetition has no meaning?
options: Raw count weighting, so a repeated tag scores proportionally higher
Logarithmic weighting, so each repeated tag still adds a smaller amount
Inverse document frequency alone, so tag rarity replaces tag presence
Binary presence weighting, since a single tag occurrence is the whole signal

questions.topic: Term Frequency and Its Saturation Problem
questions.question: Why can maximum-frequency normalization be unstable?
options: It divides each weight by the document's total token count, which drifts
One repeated unrelated term changes the divisor and rescales every weight
It leaves the most frequent term in a document with a normalized weight of zero
It depends on collection statistics that shift as new documents arrive

questions.topic: Inverse Document Frequency: Rare Terms Carry Signal
questions.question: What does document frequency measure?
options: The total number of times a term occurs in one particular document
The total number of times a term occurs across the whole collection
The number of collection documents that contain the term at least once
The number of positions recorded for the term inside a single posting list

questions.topic: Inverse Document Frequency: Rare Terms Carry Signal
questions.question: What is the core unsmoothed IDF formula?
options: log(df divided by N)
tf multiplied by df
(N minus df) over N
log(N divided by df)

questions.topic: Inverse Document Frequency: Rare Terms Carry Signal
questions.question: A term appears in every document. What is its unsmoothed IDF?
options: log N
N

questions.topic: Inverse Document Frequency: Rare Terms Carry Signal
questions.question: In 10,000 documents, vector appears in 100 and database in 1,000. How do their natural-log IDFs compare?
options: Database has twice vector's IDF
Vector has twice database's IDF
Their IDF values are identical
Both terms have an IDF of zero

questions.topic: Inverse Document Frequency: Rare Terms Carry Signal
questions.question: Why can an extremely rare term still be a poor ranking signal?
options: Document frequency counts occurrences, so rare terms are miscounted
Smoothed IDF pulls every very rare term's weight back toward zero
A term rare across the collection must also be rare within a document
It may be a typo, a random identifier, or an extraction artifact

questions.topic: Inverse Document Frequency: Rare Terms Carry Signal
questions.question: Why are scores from segment-local IDF statistics potentially inconsistent?
options: Segments store postings without any document frequency counters at all
Every segment holds an identical distribution of terms after a merge
A term can look artificially rare in a small new segment but common overall
IDF depends only on the query, so segment composition cannot change it

questions.question: What does basic tf-idf multiply?
options: A document's term frequency by that term's inverse document frequency
A document's total length by the number of terms present in the query
A term's collection frequency by the dimension of the document vector
A document's rank position by the depth at which the crawler found it

questions.question: Why can query tf be binary while document tf is logarithmic?
options: Documents repeat their own terms too rarely for a log transform to matter
A query names each term once, while document repetition carries evidence
Binary query weights supply the synonyms a logarithmic weight cannot
A logarithmic weight would drop each term a query mentions only once

questions.question: With N=10,000 and vector df=100, what is vector's natural-log IDF approximately?
Why use separate title and body weights?
options: Title text and body text carry evidence of exactly equal reliability
Field separation removes the need to analyze either field at indexing
Body term frequency can never rise above the title's term frequency
One title occurrence can outweigh several occurrences buried in a long body

questions.question: Which contribution trace best explains a lexical result?
options: Matched terms with transformed tf, idf, field boost, and each subtotal
The final floating-point score together with the document's own identifier
The crawl timestamp and the byte size of the stored source document
The rank the document held under the previous version of the index

questions.question: Why must a tf-idf model version include its statistics and formula?
options: A change to the smoothing constant cannot alter any document ordering
Reproducing a score needs the same corpus statistics and transforms
Posting lists already store the full score explanation for every query
The logarithm base used can be recovered from the document's own text
